entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Book of Joshua is the sixth book of the Hebrew Bible and the Old Testament, and the first book of the Deuteronomistic History — the scholarly designation for Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings as a continuous narrative. The book describes the Israelite conquest of Canaan under Joshua's leadership following Moses's death, the allotment of land to the twelve tribes, and Joshua's final exhortation to the Israelites to remain faithful to their covenant with YHWH.

Joshua divides into three main sections: the crossing of the Jordan and the conquest of Canaan (chapters 1–12), the distribution of the land among the twelve tribes (13–21), and Joshua's farewell speeches and the covenant at Shechem (22–24). The canonical narratives include the fall of Jericho (by divine intervention, its walls collapsing at the sound of trumpets), the sun standing still at Gibeon ('Joshua 10:12–13' — one of the Bible's most discussed miraculous texts), and the 'Herem' (total destruction) of Canaanite cities.

Scholarly analysis places the book's composition in the 7th–6th centuries BCE, during or after the Babylonian exile, as part of the Deuteronomistic redaction of Israel's history. Archaeological evidence is contested: the Jericho of the relevant period shows no evidence of destruction walls, while other sites (Lachish, Hazor) show destructions consistent with conquest narratives. For the Christian tradition, Joshua is typologically linked to Jesus — both names derive from the same Hebrew root — and the conquest of Canaan was interpreted as a prefiguration of spiritual salvation.
